newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine slows army reduction due to lack of cash.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine slows army reduction due to lack of cash.

text.p: Ukraine decided on Saturday to slow down a planned reduction in its army, Europe's second biggest after Russia's, due to a severe lack of funds but said it would press on with modernisation of its forces.
The powerful Security and Defence Council, which includes President Leonid Kuchma, the prime minister and several key ministers, approved a State Military Programme for the period up to 2005.
Military sources said the programme envisages cutting the army, currently 400,000 strong, to 350,000 by 2005, not by the end of 1996 as initially planned.
"This is a very serious step that allows the armed forces to enter the new year with clear tasks," Volodymyr Horbulin, head of the Security and Defence Council, told reporters.
The armed forces were formed shortly after the breakup of the Soviet Union from divisions deployed on Ukrainian territory. Their complement was then estimated at between 750,000 and one million.

"The state simply has no money to return servicemen to civilian life," Serhiy Zhurets, a military commentator on the Den daily, told Reuters. "Earlier statements were based on political populism rather than real calculations."
The Interior Ministry recently announced plans to reduce its troops from 52,000 to 30,000 next year.

Defence Ministry sources said the programme approved on Saturday abandoned the old Soviet system of military districts and set up three "operational commands" based in the western city of Lvov, in the Black Sea port of Odessa and in Chernihiv in the north, on the Russian border.
All three commands will have separate mobile forces and special units for international peacekeeping operations, they said.
But cash-strapped Ukraine seems unlikely to move from a conscript-based to a professional army any time soon.

"We don't foresee any transition to a professional army," Defence Minister Olexander Kuzmuk said recently. "We could consider this issue no earlier than 2005 because of the economic situation," he said.

The state budget allocated 1.5 billion hryvnia ($850 million) for the armed forces this year and 1.43 billion for 1997. Officers' monthly salaries, equivalent to less than $150, frequently go unpaid. Many officers have no proper housing.

"This means that the army's stagnation will continue. The programme cannot be realised because of a lack of financing," Zhurets said. "They pay just enough to keep the army alive and haven't allocated any money for the actual reforms."
Opinion polls show that the army remains the most trusted institution in Ukraine after the Orthodox Church.
